claims.text: Introducing a low concentration of a noble-metal dopant improves the structural stability of near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles during high-temperature catalytic operation.
Introducing a low concentration of a noble-metal dopant improves the chemical stability of these nanoparticles during high-temperature catalytic operation.
The noble-metal dopant retards atomic diffusion.
The noble-metal dopant mitigates elemental segregation.
The initial nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Local compositional homogeneity is promoted by reduced diffusion pathways.
Local compositional homogeneity is promoted by mitigation of lattice distortions.
A small amount of noble-metal dopant alters atomic-scale interactions.
Dopant-induced changes in atomic-scale interactions reduce defect formation.
Reduced defect formation slows diffusion-driven elemental segregation.
Slower diffusion-driven segregation preserves a single-phase solid solution at high temperature.
Doped nanoparticles will exhibit less phase separation than otherwise identical undoped nanoparticles after the same high-temperature treatment.
Doped nanoparticles will exhibit less compositional heterogeneity than otherwise identical undoped nanoparticles after the same high-temperature treatment.
Undoped nanoparticles are more prone to atomic diffusion and the onset of phase segregation under the stated high-temperature conditions.
The predicted stabilizing effect applies at 773–1173 K when the dopant concentration remains below its solubility limit.
The predicted trend may fail at very high dopant concentrations or at temperatures that cause melting.
